Lesson A0-03: Describing People and Family ​

Level: A0 (Foundations)
CEFR Level: A0
Duration: 90 minutes
New Vocabulary: 45 words
Grammar Focus: Demonstratives (deze, dit, die, dat); basic adjectives and agreement; possessive structures with "van"; present tense of "hebben" in descriptive context

Lesson Goal ​

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe family members and people in photographs using adjectives, demonstratives, and simple possessive structures, and ask and answer questions about family relationships and characteristics.

Previous Knowledge ​

You must have completed A0-01: Understanding Sounds and A0-02: Introducing Yourself before starting this lesson.

From A0-01 and A0-02, you should know:

  • Dutch alphabet and pronunciation (all vowel and consonant sounds)
  • Personal pronouns (ik, jij, hij, zij, het, u, wij, jullie, zij)
  • Present tense of "zijn" (ben, bent, is, zijn)
  • Present tense of "hebben" (heb, hebt, heeft, hebben)
  • Simple yes/no questions with inversion
  • de/het articles and basic word order
  • Possessive pronouns (mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons, jullie, hun)
  • A0-02 vocabulary: family (moeder, vader, broer, zus), countries, nationalities, languages, numbers 0-20

This lesson builds on your understanding of "zijn," "hebben," and articles to introduce new ways to describe people and their relationships.

Why This Matters ​

In real conversations, people rarely just say "This is my grandmother." They describe them: "This is my grandmother. She is old and very kind." You need adjectives, demonstratives ("this" and "that"), and ways to talk about possession and relationships. This lesson teaches you the grammar and vocabulary to bring people to life in conversation--to describe family photos, answer questions about relatives, and create the detailed, natural descriptions that make conversations meaningful.

Grammar ​

This lesson introduces six core grammar concepts for describing people and relationships:

1. Demonstratives: Deze, Dit, Die, Dat ​

Explanation

Dutch has four demonstratives: "deze" and "dit" for "this/these" (nearby), and "die" and "dat" for "that/those" (far). Which form you use depends on two things:

  1. Distance: Near (deze/dit) or far (die/dat)
  2. Article of the noun: de-word, het-word, or plural

Selection Pattern:

ArticleNearFar
de (singular)dezedie
het (singular)ditdat
plural (all)dezedie

Why it matters: Demonstratives let you point out specific people in photos or conversations: "Deze tante is aardig" (This aunt is nice), "Dat kind is jong" (That child is young).

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Deze tante is aardig.This aunt is nice.
Dit kind is jong.This child is young.
Die oom is lang.That uncle is tall.
Dat meisje is klein.That girl is small.
Deze mensen zijn blij.These people are happy.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ deze kind → ✅ dit kind (kind is a het-word, so use "dit")
  • ❌ dit mensen → ✅ deze mensen (plurals use deze/die, not dit/dat)
  • ❌ Deze zijn mijn ouders → ✅ Dit zijn mijn ouders / Dat zijn mijn ouders (Use the neutral pattern with this/that for introducing multiple people)

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 taught you de/het articles. A0-03 uses that knowledge to choose the right demonstrative. You already know the system; now you're applying it.

2. Basic Adjectives and Their Position ​

Explanation

Dutch adjectives can come in two positions:

  1. Predicative: After the verb "zijn" → adjective stays in base form (no ending)
  2. Attributive: Before the noun → adjective usually adds an ending (usually "-e")

Why it matters: You need both positions to describe naturally: "De oma is oud" (predicate: The grandma is old) and "De oude oma is aardig" (attribute: The old grandma is nice).

Pattern:

  • After zijn: De oma is oud. (no change)
  • Before noun: De oude oma is aardig. (add -e)

Examples:

DutchEnglish
De oma is oud.The grandmother is old.
De oude oma is aardig.The old grandmother is nice.
Het kind is jong.The child is young.
Het jonge kind is blij.The young child is happy.
De neef is grappig.The cousin is funny.
De grappige neef is lief.The funny cousin is sweet.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ De tante is vriendelijke → ✅ De tante is vriendelijk (Don't add -e after "zijn")
  • ❌ de oud opa → ✅ de oude opa (Add -e before the noun)

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 used "zijn" only for simple identity and nationality (Ik ben Nederlands). A0-03 uses "zijn" + adjectives to describe characteristics (De opa is oud).

3. Adjective Agreement: Simplified -e Rules ​

Explanation

For A0, here is the core rule: Before a noun, add "-e" to the adjective almost always. The main exception is "een + singular het-word," where the adjective stays bare.

The Core Rule:

  • Before "de" noun: Add -e. de oude opa
  • Before "het" noun: Add -e. het jonge kind
  • Before plural: Add -e. de oude opa's (grandpas)
  • Exception: "een" + singular het-word: No -e. een jong kind (not "een jonge kind")

Light Spelling Changes:

When you add "-e," some adjectives change their spelling slightly:

  • wit → witte (double t)
  • rood → rode (d stays)
  • groen → groene (n stays)

Adjectives already ending in "-e" (like oranje, roze) don't get another "-e."

Why it matters: Correct agreement sounds natural and is necessary for fluent Dutch: "de vriendelijke tante" (the friendly aunt), "het jonge kind" (the young child), "een jong kind" (a young child).

Examples:

DutchEnglish
de oude opathe old grandfather
het jonge kindthe young child
een jong kinda young child
de kleine kinderenthe small children
dit vriendelijke meisjethis friendly girl

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ een jonge kind → ✅ een jong kind (Exception: no -e with een + het singular)
  • ❌ het jong kind → ✅ het jonge kind (Before het noun, add -e)
  • ❌ de wit foto → ✅ de witte foto (Double the t when adding -e to wit)

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 focused on articles themselves (de/het). A0-03 shows how articles affect what comes after them, including adjectives. It's a new application of old knowledge.

4. Singular Nouns with Articles: De and Het ​

Explanation

Dutch has two singular articles: "de" for common-gender nouns and "het" for neuter nouns. All plurals use "de." This is a review from A0-02, but now you apply it to family and descriptive vocabulary.

Why it matters: The article determines which demonstrative you use (deze/dit or die/dat), and whether an adjective gets -e before the noun.

Key Nouns for This Lesson:

  • de: tante (aunt), oom (uncle), opa (grandpa), oma (grandma), neef (cousin), niet (cousin-female), foto (photo), bril (glasses), baard (beard), persoon (person)
  • het: kind (child), kleinkind (grandchild), haar (hair)
  • Plural: opa's, tantes, kinderen, foto's

Examples:

DutchEnglish
de tantethe aunt
het kindthe child
een ooman uncle
de fotothe photo
het haarthe hair

Common mistakes:

  • Learning nouns without articles. Always teach and learn: "het kind," not just "kind."
  • Forgetting that plurals always take "de."

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 introduced de/het. A0-03 reviews and applies this knowledge to new family vocabulary and ensures you understand that articles are the foundation for other grammar choices (demonstratives, adjective agreement).

5. Possessive Structures Using "Van" ​

Explanation

The everyday Dutch way to express possession is: [noun/person] + van + [owner], literally "the X of Y." This is equivalent to English possessive ('s): "the mother of Anna" = "Anna's mother."

Pattern:

[article + noun] + van + [person/possessor]

Why it matters: This structure is safe and reliable for A0 learners. It avoids the need to master all possessive pronouns and offers a clear alternative: instead of "haar moeder" (her mother), you can always say "de moeder van Anna."

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Dit is de moeder van Anna.This is Anna's mother.
Dat is de oom van Sara.That is Sara's uncle.
De bril van opa is zwart.Grandpa's glasses are black.
De foto van de familie is mooi.The family photo is beautiful.
De broer van mijn moeder is mijn oom.My mother's brother is my uncle.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Anna moeder → ✅ de moeder van Anna (You must use "van" and the article)
  • ❌ de moeder van Anna is oud (missing verb)
  • ❌ moeder Anna → ✅ de moeder van Anna

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 introduced possessive pronouns (mijn, jouw, zijn, haar). A0-03 adds a noun-based possession pattern that many learners find easier: instead of choosing the right pronoun, you just use a person's name with "van."

6. Present Tense of "Hebben" (To Have) in Possession Context ​

Explanation

Use "hebben" to say who has people, objects, or features. This is a review from A0-02, but now you apply it to describing appearance and possessions: "Zij heeft lang haar" (She has long hair), "Hij heeft een bril" (He has glasses).

Conjugation (Review from A0-02):

PronounFormExample
ikhebIk heb een opa. (I have a grandfather.)
jij/jehebtJij hebt een tante. (You have an aunt.)
uhebt / heeftU hebt/heeft een familie. (You have a family.)
hij/zij/hetheeftZij heeft lang haar. (She has long hair.)
wij/wehebbenWij hebben een grote familie. (We have a big family.)
julliehebbenJullie hebben broers en zussen. (You all have brothers and sisters.)
zij/zehebbenZij hebben een baard. (They have a beard.)

Why it matters: Many physical descriptions and family relationships require "hebben": "Mijn opa heeft wit haar" (My grandpa has white hair), "Mijn nicht heeft een bril" (My cousin has glasses).

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Ik heb een tante.I have an aunt.
Hij heeft een bril.He has glasses.
Zij heeft lang haar.She has long hair.
Wij hebben een grote familie.We have a big family.
Heb jij een broer?Do you have a brother?

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Hij hebt → ✅ Hij heeft (hij takes "heeft," not "hebt")
  • ❌ Hebt jij…? → ✅ Heb jij…? (jij takes "heb" in questions, not "hebt")
  • ❌ Ik hebben → ✅ Ik heb (ik takes "heb")

Contrast with A0-02:

A0-02 introduced "hebben" for basic possession: "Ik heb een broer." A0-03 uses it in the same way but extends it to describe appearance: "Zij heeft lang haar" (She has long hair).

Grammar Reasoning ​

Why Demonstratives Matter ​

English speakers are used to just saying "this" or "that" without worrying about the noun's gender. Dutch forces you to think about the noun's article, which keeps you aware of gender throughout your speech. This is extra work at first, but it trains you to be precise.

Why Adjective Agreement Is Different from English ​

English adjectives never change: "the old man," "the old woman," "the old men." Dutch adjectives change to agree with the noun. This is normal in many European languages (Spanish, French, German all do this). The pattern is predictable: before a noun, you usually add "-e." After "zijn," the adjective stays bare.

Why "Van" Possession Is Easier Than All Pronoun Forms ​

Instead of memorizing when to use "zijn," "haar," "hun," and so on, you can always use "van + name." "De moeder van Anna" is unambiguous and safe. As your Dutch improves, you'll use pronouns more, but starting with "van" is smart.

Why "Hebben" Appears in Descriptions ​

English says "She is blonde" (using "is" + adjective). Dutch often says "Zij heeft blond haar" (She has blonde hair, using "hebben" + noun). This is a different pattern, so pay attention: physical features often use "hebben" in Dutch, not just "zijn."

Pronunciation ​

Dutch adjectives, colors, and demonstratives have clear, predictable pronunciation once you know the vowel sounds from A0-01.

Demonstratives ​

  • deze (DAY-zuh) -- Like "day" + "zuh"
  • dit (DIT) -- Short i + t
  • die (DEE) -- Long i, like "see" with d
  • dat (DAHT) -- Short a + t

Common Adjectives ​

  • groot (KHROHT) -- Like "throat" with kh
  • klein (KLINE) -- Like "line" with k
  • oud (OWT) -- Like "out" with different vowel
  • jong (YONG) -- Like "young" with j
  • vriendelijk (VREEN-duh-luk) -- Three syllables; first two run together
  • aardig (AHR-dukh) -- First syllable stressed
  • lief (LEEF) -- Long e sound
  • slim (SLIM) -- Short i
  • grappig (KHRAH-pukh) -- First syllable stressed
  • mooi (MOY) -- Like "boy" but with m
  • lelijk (LAY-luk) -- First syllable stressed
  • blij (BLY) -- Like "buy" with b
  • verdrietig (ver-DREET-ukh) -- Four syllables; first two run together
  • rustig (RUS-tuk) -- First syllable stressed

Colors ​

  • rood (ROHT) -- Like "road"
  • blauw (BLOW) -- Like "blue" in English
  • groen (KHROON) -- Like "rune" with kh
  • geel (KHAYL) -- Like "hale" with kh
  • wit (VIT) -- Short i + t
  • zwart (ZVAHRT) -- Like "heart" with zv at start
  • bruin (BROWN) -- Like "brown"
  • oranje (oh-RAHN-yuh) -- Three syllables; stress second syllable
  • roze (ROH-zuh) -- Like "rose" + "uh"
  • paars (PAHRS) -- Like "cars" with p

Family Words ​

  • opa (OH-pah) -- Short o
  • oma (OH-mah) -- Short o
  • tante (TAHN-tuh) -- First syllable stressed
  • oom (OHM) -- Long o
  • neef (NAYF) -- Like "safe" with n
  • nicht (NIKHT) -- Short i + kht
  • kleinkind (KLINE-kint) -- Two syllables run together

Dialogue ​

Here are four realistic dialogues showing how to describe family and people using adjectives, demonstratives, and possession.

Dialogue 1: Describing a Family Member ​

Dutch:

A: Wie is dit?
B: Dit is mijn oma. Zij is oud en aardig.
A: Heeft zij wit haar?
B: Ja, zij heeft wit haar.

Translation:

A: Who is this?
B: This is my grandma. She is old and nice.
A: Does she have white hair?
B: Yes, she has white hair.

Dialogue 2: Identifying People in a Photo ​

Dutch:

A: Is deze man je oom?
B: Ja, deze man is mijn oom.
A: En die vrouw?
B: Die vrouw is de tante van Anna.

Translation:

A: Is this man your uncle?
B: Yes, this man is my uncle.
A: And that woman?
B: That woman is Anna's aunt.

Dialogue 3: Asking About Relationships ​

Dutch:

A: Wie is dat kind?
B: Dat is het kleinkind van opa.
A: Is het kind jong?
B: Ja, het kind is jong en blij.

Translation:

A: Who is that child?
B: That is grandpa's grandchild.
A: Is the child young?
B: Yes, the child is young and happy.

Dialogue 4: Appearance ​

Dutch:

A: Heeft je neef lang haar?
B: Nee, hij heeft kort haar.
A: Heeft hij een bril?
B: Ja, hij heeft een zwarte bril.

Translation:

A: Does your cousin have long hair?
B: No, he has short hair.
A: Does he have glasses?
B: Yes, he has black glasses.

Reading ​

Read this short text about describing a family. It uses only grammar and vocabulary you've learned in A0-01, A0-02, and A0-03.

Dutch Text:

Dit is de foto van mijn familie. Dit is mijn opa. Hij is oud en rustig. Hij heeft wit haar. Dat is mijn oma. Zij is oud en aardig. Zij heeft kort haar.

Dit is mijn vader. Hij is groot en grappig. Die vrouw is mijn moeder. Zij is vriendelijk en mooi. Zij heeft lang bruin haar.

Dit is mijn broer. Hij is jong en slim. Die meisje is mijn zus. Zij is blij en lief.

Deze foto is mooi. Mijn familie is groot en gelukkig.

English Translation:

This is the photo of my family. This is my grandpa. He is old and calm. He has white hair. That is my grandma. She is old and nice. She has short hair.

This is my father. He is big and funny. That woman is my mother. She is friendly and beautiful. She has long brown hair.

This is my brother. He is young and smart. That girl is my sister. She is happy and sweet.

This photo is beautiful. My family is big and happy.

Listen to these short conversations about describing family. You can read the transcripts below. Try to understand as much as you can before reading the translations.

Conversation 1:

[Audio would be located at /shared/assets/audio/A0-03-listening-01.mp3]

A: Is hij vriendelijk?

Translation:

A: Does he have a beard?

A: Is he friendly?
B: Yes, he is very friendly.

Comprehension Questions:

  1. Wie is de man? (Who is the man?)
    Answer: De opa (The grandpa)

  2. Heeft hij een baard? (Does he have a beard?)
    Answer: Ja (Yes)

  3. Wat kleur is de baard? (What color is the beard?)

[Audio would be located at /shared/assets/audio/A0-03-listening-02.mp3]

A: Heeft hij lang haar?

B: Ja, hij is grappig en vriendelijk.

    Answer: De neef (The cousin)

  2. Heeft hij lang haar? (Does he have long hair?)
    Answer: Nee, hij heeft kort haar (No, he has short hair)

  3. Wat heeft hij nog? (What else does he have?)
    Answer: Een bril (Glasses)

Speaking ​

Practice describing family members and people in photographs using adjectives, demonstratives, and possession.

Exercise 1: Informal Description ​

Scenario: You're showing a family photo to a classmate.

What you say:

  1. Point to someone: "Dit is mijn [family member]."
  2. Describe them: "[He/She] is [adjective]."
  3. Add a detail: "[He/She] has [noun] + color/length."

Model Response:

"Dit is mijn oma. Zij is oud en aardig. Zij heeft wit haar."

Exercise 2: Describing Multiple People ​

Scenario: Someone asks about people in a photo.

They ask: "Wie is deze man?"
You respond: "Dit is mijn opa. Hij is oud en grappig."

They ask: "En die vrouw?"
You respond: "Die vrouw is mijn oma. Zij is vriendelijk."

They ask: "Zijn zij aardig?"
You respond: "Ja, zij zijn zeer aardig."

Exercise 3: Appearance Questions ​

Scenario: A partner asks about someone's appearance.

They ask: "Heeft je broer lang haar?"
You respond: "Nee, hij heeft kort haar."

They ask: "Heeft hij een bril?"
You respond: "Ja, hij heeft een blauwe bril."

They ask: "Is hij grappig?"
You respond: "Ja, hij is grappig en slim."

Exercise 4: Demonstrative Practice ​

Scenario: Point out different people using demonstratives.

Situation 1: This person is near you.
"Deze tante is aardig. Zij heeft lang bruin haar."

Situation 2: That person is far from you.
"Die oom is groot en grappig. Heeft hij een baard?"

Situation 3: This child is near you (het-word).
"Dit kind is jong en blij. Het kind is lief."

Writing ​

Exercise 1: Fill in the Blanks -- Adjectives and Demonstratives ​

Complete each sentence with the correct adjective or demonstrative form.

  1. ___ tante is aardig. (near + de-word) → Deze
  2. Dit kind is ___. (young) → jong
  3. De ___ opa is rustig. (old + adjective form) → oude
  4. Zij heeft ___ haar. (long) → lang
  5. ___ meisje is blij. (that + het-word) → Dat
  6. De broer van mijn moeder is mijn ___. (relationship) → oom
  7. Het ___ kind is lief. (young + adjective form) → jonge
  8. ___ mensen zijn vriendelijk. (these) → Deze
  9. De foto van de ___ is mooi. (family) → familie
  10. Mijn opa heeft ___ haar. (white) → wit

Answers: 1. Deze 2. jong 3. oude 4. lang 5. Dat 6. oom 7. jonge 8. Deze 9. familie 10. wit

Exercise 2: Demonstrative Agreement ​

Rewrite each phrase using the correct demonstrative (deze/dit/die/dat).

  1. This aunt (nearby) → Deze tante
  2. That child (far, het-word) → Dat kind
  3. These people (nearby) → Deze mensen
  4. That uncle (far) → Die oom
  5. This photo (nearby) → Deze foto
  6. That hair (far, het-word) → Dat haar
  7. These friends (nearby) → Deze vrienden
  8. That beard (far) → Die baard

Exercise 3: Adjective Agreement ​

Add the correct form of the adjective to each phrase.

  1. een jong kind (a young child) -- jong, jong
  2. de oude opa (the old grandfather) -- oud, oude
  3. het mooie huis (the beautiful house) -- mooi, mooie
  4. een vriendelijke tante (a friendly aunt) -- vriendelijk, vriendelijke
  5. de grote man (the big man) -- groot, grote
  6. het kleine meisje (the small girl) -- klein, kleine
  7. een grappige oom (a funny uncle) -- grappig, grappige
  8. de blije kinderen (the happy children) -- blij, blije

Exercise 4: Possession with "Van" ​

Rewrite each sentence using "van" structure.

  1. My grandpa's beard → De baard van mijn opa
  2. Anna's mother → De moeder van Anna
  3. The family's photo → De foto van de familie
  4. My cousin's glasses → De bril van mijn neef
  5. Your uncle's house → Het huis van je oom

Exercise 5: Self-Introduction Paragraph ​

Write a short paragraph (5-7 sentences) describing your family or a family member. Include:

  • Who you're describing (demonstrative + name/relationship)
  • At least 3 adjectives
  • At least one physical feature (using "hebben")
  • One possession (using "van")

Requirement: Use correct adjective forms and demonstratives.

Model Answer:

Dit is mijn opa. De opa is oud en rustig. Hij heeft wit haar. De baard van opa is grijs. Mijn opa is zeer vriendelijk. Hij is aardig en grappig. Ik hou van mijn opa.

Common Mistakes ​

Mistake 1: Confusing Demonstratives ​

Wrong: deze kind / dit tante
Right: dit kind / deze tante
Why: Use "dit/dat" with het-words (singular); use "deze/die" with de-words and plural nouns.

Mistake 2: Forgetting Adjective -E in Attributive Position ​

Wrong: de oud opa / het jong kind
Right: de oude opa / het jonge kind
Why: Before a noun, add "-e" to adjectives (except een + het-word singular).

Mistake 3: Adding -E After "Zijn" ​

Wrong: De oma is aardig-e. / Het kind is blij-e.
Right: De oma is aardig. / Het kind is blij.
Why: After "zijn," adjectives stay in base form. No ending needed.

Mistake 4: Using "Een" + Adjective -E Incorrectly ​

Wrong: een jonge kind
Right: een jong kind
Why: With "een" + singular het-word, don't add "-e."

Mistake 5: Confusing Possession Patterns ​

Wrong: opa bril / de bril opa
Right: de bril van opa
Why: Always use "van" for possession: [article + noun] + van + [possessor].

Mistake 6: Not Conjugating "Hebben" Correctly ​

Wrong: Hij hebt / Zij hebben kort haar.
Right: Hij heeft / Zij hebben kort haar.
Why: Each pronoun requires the correct form: hij/zij takes "heeft"; wij/jullie/zij takes "hebben."

Mistake 7: Confusing "Lang" (Tall/Long) and "Kort" (Short) ​

Wrong: De opa is kort. (means "The grandpa is short.")
Right: De opa heeft lang haar. (means "The grandpa has long hair.")
Why: "Lang/kort" describes hair length; "groot/klein" describes body size. Use context to choose.

Mistake 8: Color Spelling with -E ​

Wrong: de wite foto
Right: de witte foto
Why: When adding "-e" to "wit," double the "t": wit → witte.

Dutch Insight ​

Dutch Family Structures ​

The Netherlands recognizes many family structures: nuclear families (two parents and children), single-parent families, blended families (remarriage), same-sex couples with children, and multigenerational households. When describing family, Dutch people are matter-of-fact about all these structures. You won't offend anyone by asking "Wie is dit?" (Who is this?) if you're not sure of the relationship.

How Dutch People Describe Others ​

Dutch culture values directness, but not rudeness. When describing people, Dutch speakers tend to emphasize personality and character traits (aardig, vriendelijk, grappig) rather than appearance. Comments about weight, age, or attractiveness can be considered impolite unless you know someone very well. Safe descriptive adjectives: friendly, kind, nice, funny, smart, calm. Less safe: focusing on body type, age, or beauty.

Photo Conversation Norms ​

Family photos are a common conversation starter in Dutch homes and social settings. It's polite to ask "Wie is dit?" and listen to the story. Phrases like "De foto is mooi" (The photo is beautiful) are always appropriate.

Non-Verbal Etiquette ​

In some cultures, pointing with one finger at a person is normal. In Dutch culture, it can seem rude or overly direct. In classroom role-plays, use "in deze foto" / "op de foto" (in/on this photo) instead of physically pointing.

Memory Tricks ​

Trick 1: Demonstratives by Distance and Gender ​

DEZE/DIT = NEAR (sounds like "these" in English)
DIE/DAT = FAR (sounds like "that")

  • If the noun is de-word: use deze (near) or die (far)
  • If the noun is het-word: use dit (near) or dat (far)
  • If plural: use deze (near) or die (far)

Memory rhyme: "Deze and Die for words we see, Dit and Dat for the rest, you see!"

Trick 2: Adjective -E Rule ​

AFTER ZIJN = NO -E
"De opa is oud." (bare form)

BEFORE NOUN = ADD -E (almost always)
"De oude opa." (with -e)

Exception: "een + het-word = NO -E"
"een jong kind" (not "een jonge kind")

Think of it like a formula:

  • Predicative (after zijn): bare
  • Attributive (before de/het/plural): +e
  • Exception: een + het-singular: bare

Trick 3: "Van" Possession ​

Instead of memorizing all possessive pronouns, use "van":

  • English: "My mother's photo"
  • Dutch: "De foto van mijn moeder" (The photo of my mother)

You already know "van" (from = origin), so reuse it for possession too!

Trick 4: Colors as Adjectives ​

Colors are adjectives, so they follow the same -e rule:

  • After zijn: bare → "De bril is zwart."
  • Before noun: +e → "De zwarte bril."

Double the final consonant if it's a single consonant preceded by a single vowel:

  • wit → witte (double t)
  • rood → rode (already has oo, so just add -e)

Trick 5: "Lang" vs "Groot" ​

  • Lang = tall (for people) or long (for hair/objects)
  • Groot = big (for objects) or tall (for people size)
  • Kort = short (for hair/height)
  • Klein = small (for objects/people)

Context clue: If it's with "haar," it's probably "lang" or "kort."

Active Recall ​

Do NOT look at the answers yet. Write or say your responses.

  1. What are the four Dutch demonstratives, and when do you use each?

  2. Why do adjectives change form before a noun but not after "zijn"?

  3. Write the correct demonstrative: "This aunt" (nearby) = ___ tante.

  4. Write the correct adjective form: The old grandfather = De ___ opa.

  5. Fill in the van-possession structure: Anna's mother = De ___ van ___.

  6. How would you ask "Does he have long hair?" in Dutch?

  7. What is the color of this item? (Point to something and name its color in Dutch.)

  8. How do you describe a family member's appearance using hebben? Give one example.

  9. What is the exception to the -e adjective rule?

  10. Translate to Dutch: "These people are friendly."

Answers:

  1. Four demonstratives:

    • deze (near + de-word or plural)
    • dit (near + het-word)
    • die (far + de-word or plural)
    • dat (far + het-word)

  2. Why adjectives change: Because Dutch nouns have gender (de/het), and adjectives must agree. After "zijn," adjectives are predicative (not modifying the noun directly), so no agreement marker needed. Before a noun (attributive), the adjective modifies the noun, so it agrees with the noun's gender/number.

  3. This aunt (nearby, de-word): Deze tante.

  4. The old grandfather: De oude opa. (Add -e before the noun.)

  5. Anna's mother: De moeder van Anna.

  6. "Does he have long hair?" Heeft hij lang haar?

  7. Your answer will depend on the object. Example: "Dit is rood" (This is red) or "De bril is blauw" (The glasses are blue).

  8. Example with hebben: "Zij heeft wit haar" (She has white hair) or "Hij heeft een baard" (He has a beard).

  9. Exception to -e rule: "een" + singular het-word takes no -e. Example: "een jong kind" (a young child), not "een jonge kind."

  10. "These people are friendly." Deze mensen zijn vriendelijk. OR Dat zijn vriendelijke mensen.

Quiz ​

Read each question. Write or say your answer. Then check the Answer Key below.

Question 1: Which demonstrative goes with "het kind" (this, near)? ​

A) deze
B) dit
C) die
D) dat

Correct Answer: B) it (het-word, so use "dit")

Question 2: How do you say "the old grandmother" in Dutch? ​

A) de oud oma
B) de oude oma
C) de oma oud
D) oud de oma

Correct Answer: B) de oude oma (Add -e before the noun in attributive position)

Question 3: Complete: "Mijn tante ___ vriendelijk." ​

A) heeft
B) heb
C) is
D) ben

Correct Answer: C) is (Personality traits use "zijn," not "hebben")

Question 4: How do you express "My uncle's photo" using "van"? ​

A) Mijn oom foto
B) De foto mijn oom
C) De foto van mijn oom
D) Mijn foto van oom

Correct Answer: C) De foto van mijn oom

Question 5: Which is correct for "a young child"? ​

A) een jonge kind
B) een jong kind
C) een jonge het kind
D) een jong het kind

Correct Answer: B) een jong kind (Exception: een + het-word singular = no -e)

Question 6: "That woman" (far, de-word) = ___ ​

A) dit vrouw
B) die vrouw
C) dat vrouw
D) deze vrouw

Correct Answer: B) die vrouw (far + de-word = die)

Question 7: What is the correct form of the adjective after "zijn"? ​

A) With -e added
B) In base form (no ending)
C) With -ed added
D) The same as before a noun

Correct Answer: B) In base form (no ending) (Predicative adjectives don't get -e)

Question 8: How many grandchildren does he have? (Expressing possession) ​

Dutch: "Hoeveel ___ hij?" / "Hij ___ vier ___."

A) hebt / heb / kleinkind
B) heeft / heb / kleinkinden
C) heeft / heeft / kleinkinden
D) hebben / heb / kleinkind

Correct Answer: C) heeft / heeft / kleinkinden (hij has "heeft" in both positions; plural of kleinkind is kleinkinderen)

Question 9: "Does she have long hair?" = ___ ​

A) Heeft zij lang haar?
B) Is zij lang haar?
C) Zij heeft lang haar?
D) Lang haar zij heeft?

Correct Answer: A) Heeft zij lang haar? (Inversion for questions; physical features use hebben + noun, not zijn + adjective)

Question 10: What color is the article "het haar" (hair)? ​

A) het is een kleur
B) het is geen kleur
C) het kan wit, zwart, bruin, rood zijn
D) alles above

Correct Answer: C) het kan wit, zwart, bruin, rood zijn (Hair can be white, black, brown, red, etc.)

Question 11: "De tante van Anna" literally means: ​

A) Anna's sister
B) The aunt of Anna / Anna's aunt
C) The aunt and Anna
D) Anna has an aunt

Correct Answer: B) The aunt of Anna / Anna's aunt

Question 12: Complete: "Deze mannen zijn ___." (Fill in: "tall") ​

A) groot
B) lange
C) groote
D) groten

Correct Answer: A) groot (Predicative after zijn = base form, no -e)

Question 13: How do you say "black glasses"? ​

A) zwarte bril
B) een zwart bril
C) zwart bril
D) de zwarte bril

Correct Answer: D) de zwarte bril (Most common; with article, add -e to adjective)

Question 14: "Die kind" is incorrect. Why? ​

A) Because "kind" takes "dit," not "die"
B) Because "die" is for de-words, and "kind" is het-word
C) Because "die" is for far, and it should be near
D) Because pronouns don't combine with "die"

Correct Answer: B) Because "die" is for de-words, and "kind" is het-word (Use "dat" for far + het-word)

Question 15: What is one way to describe someone's physical appearance in Dutch? ​

A) Only using adjectives after "zijn"
B) Only using "hebben" + noun (e.g., "hij heeft lange benen")
C) Using "hebben" for features/objects, "zijn" for qualities
D) Using colors with "zijn" only

Correct Answer: C) Using "hebben" for features/objects, "zijn" for qualities (E.g., "Zij heeft lang haar" [she has long hair] vs "Zij is vriendelijk" [she is friendly])

Summary ​

Congratulations! You've completed A0-03: Describing People and Family.

Key Takeaways ​

You now know:

  • ✓ The four Dutch demonstratives (deze, dit, die, dat) and when to use each
  • ✓ How to place adjectives in both predicative and attributive positions
  • ✓ The simplified -e adjective agreement rule (before nouns, add -e; after zijn, no -e; exception: een + het-word)
  • ✓ How to use "van" for possession ("de moeder van Anna")
  • ✓ How to describe appearance and possession using "hebben" + noun
  • ✓ 45 new vocabulary words: extended family, adjectives, colors, demonstratives, physical descriptors

What You Can Do Now ​

After this lesson, you can:

  • Describe family members and people in photographs using adjectives and demonstratives
  • Ask and answer questions about family relationships and physical features
  • Use correct adjective forms in both predicative and attributive positions
  • Express possession using "van" structures or possessive pronouns from A0-02
  • Identify and describe colors in Dutch
  • Produce simple descriptive paragraphs about people you know

What Comes Next ​

The next lesson is A0-04: Greeting and Basic Politeness. You'll learn:

  • Greetings appropriate for different times of day
  • Politeness formulas (please, thank you, excuse me)
  • How to ask how someone is and respond appropriately
  • Leave-taking expressions (goodbye, see you later)
  • Imperative forms for basic commands

In that lesson, you'll practice real-world interactions: "Goedemorgen! Hoe gaat het met je?" (Good morning! How are you?) and "Dank je wel!" (Thank you!).

Study Tips for Retention ​

  1. Reread the Dialogue section 3 times. Familiar dialogues lock in new grammar.
  2. Practice demonstratives aloud every day for a week. The near/far distinction becomes automatic with repetition.
  3. Draw or find family photos and describe them in Dutch using the new adjectives and structures.
  4. Write one descriptive sentence each day using a different adjective and demonstrative.
  5. Watch Dutch family-themed videos (if available). Hearing native speakers describe family helps your ear adapt.
